---
title: "Left, right and the centre"
description: "Where young people in the UK place themselves on the left-right scale, and how this differs by age and gender."
date: 2026-11-24
categories: [Ideology, Age, Gender]
image: thumbnail.png
---





Left and right remain the most common shorthand for describing political positions, even though it is not obvious that young people, and especially adolescents, think about politics in these terms. In all four surveys, we asked respondents to place themselves on a scale from 0 (left) to 10 (right). In this article, we look at how they answered and at whether their answers differ with age and between young women and young men.

## Most answers are close to the centre

::: {.how-to-read}
Each panel shows one survey. The bars give the share of respondents who chose each point of the scale.
:::


::: {.cell layout-align="left"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/plot-distribution-1.png){fig-align='left' fig-alt='Bar charts of left-right self-placement from 0 to 10 for each of the four surveys. In every survey the middle point 5 is the most common answer. Survation W1 has more answers on the right side of the scale than the other three surveys.' width=768}
:::
:::


Across the four surveys, 49% of respondents placed themselves somewhere between 4 and 6, and the exact middle of the scale was by far the most common answer. This was particularly true of the youngest respondents, 38% of whom chose the midpoint among those aged 12 to 15, compared with 29% among those aged 18 and over. For some, choosing the middle will reflect a genuinely moderate position. For others, it may rather indicate that they do not (yet) think about politics in terms of left and right, which is one reason why averages on this scale should be read with some care.

The average positions in Gallup W1 (4.4), Gallup W2 (5.0) and Survation W2 (5.0) lie close to each other, whereas Survation W1 stands out with an average of 6.1. We do not think that this reflects a real shift to the right among younger adolescents. Respondents in Survation W1 gave higher answers on all scales running from 0 to 10, not only on this one, and those among them who took part again a year later placed themselves much like respondents in the other surveys. The difference thus seems to come from who took part in that survey rather than from what young people of that age think (see [The data](/data.qmd)).

## Age

::: {.how-to-read}
Each dot is the average position at one year of age in one survey, with a line for its 95% confidence interval. Ages with fewer than 20 respondents in a survey are left out.
:::


::: {.cell layout-align="left"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/plot-age-1.png){fig-align='left' fig-alt='Average left-right position by year of age, from 12 to 26, for each survey. Within Gallup W1 and both Survation surveys the averages change little with age. Within Gallup W2 they rise from about 4 at ages 16 and 17 to about 5.5 to 6 at ages 25 and 26. Survation W1 lies above the other surveys at every age.' width=768}
:::
:::


Within Gallup W1 and the two Survation surveys, the average position hardly changes with age. The clearest age pattern appears in Gallup W2, the only survey that covers the full range from 16 to 26. There, the average rises from 4.0 among 16 and 17 year olds to 4.5 among 18 to 21 year olds and 5.5 among those aged 22 to 26. Whether this reflects young people moving to the right as they grow older or differences between generations, a single survey cannot tell. Since the surveys cover different age ranges, a curve drawn across all ages from 12 to 26 would also mix differences between ages with differences between surveys.

## Gender

::: {.how-to-read}
Each row compares the average position of young women and young men in one age group of one survey. A longer line means a larger gap. Groups with fewer than 20 respondents are left out.
:::


::: {.cell layout-align="left"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/plot-gender-1.png){fig-align='left' fig-alt='Dumbbell chart of the average left-right position of young women and young men by survey and age group. In every row, young women place themselves further left than young men. The gap is smallest among 12 to 15 year olds and largest among 18 to 21 year olds.' width=768}
:::
:::


The gender difference is the most consistent pattern in these data. In every survey and in every age group, young women place themselves further to the left than young men. At the same time, the size of the gap changes with age. Pooled over the surveys, it amounts to only 0.2 points among 12 to 15 year olds, but grows to 0.6 points among 16 and 17 year olds and 0.8 points among 18 to 21 year olds, before narrowing slightly to 0.5 points among those aged 22 to 26. The ideological gap between young women and young men thus seems to open up during the late teens, a period that research on political socialisation regards as formative for political attitudes.

## Left and right, progressive and conservative

Three of the four surveys also asked respondents where they place themselves between socially progressive (0) and socially conservative (10). Answers on the two scales are related, with a correlation of 0.48, so that young people who see themselves on the left also tend to describe themselves as progressive. However, the relationship is far from perfect, which suggests that, for many young people, social values and a position on the left-right scale do not fully coincide. You can compare both scales by age, gender and survey in the [explorer](/explore.qmd).

## About these data

The four surveys differ in the ages they cover, in how respondents were recruited and in when they took place, and the data are not weighted. Survation respondents were between 12 and 18 years old and took part through a parent, whereas Gallup respondents were between 16 and 26 and members of an online panel. Differences between the surveys can therefore reflect who took part as much as real differences between groups of young people, which is why we mostly compare groups within the same survey. We describe the design of the surveys in more detail on [The data](/data.qmd) page.
